\title{Does Localization Tell Us Where to Repair a Shortcut? A Study with a Planted Shortcut in GPT-2}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Interpretability tools can show where a behaviour happens inside a language model, but what does that location predict
about where a repair will work? We plant a shortcut with known ground truth: GPT-2 small learns IMDB sentiment while
an invented actor name always comes with the same label. The logit lens, block swaps and activation patching agree
that the name reaches the answer only in the last three blocks. We retrain single transformer blocks on clean data
that shows each name with both labels, and count a repair as passing our mitigation criterion when the shortcut gap at
least halves while clean accuracy falls by at most two percentage points. In the fully fine-tuned models every single
block passes after one epoch, including blocks far from the located ones. Under limited training the blocks differ:
block~0 and the later blocks are fastest, a pattern noticed post hoc and confirmed by a registered test on two new
seeds under the same settings. The swap ranking tracks this variation closely (Spearman \lThreeSpearmanFullFTRange{}
with a small repair), but localization does not consistently identify the best block or single out block~0, whose
repair, patching shows, is largely carried by the name-token states it passes on. The correlation is weaker under
LoRA. In Pythia-160M every single block passes when retrained with counter-examples. In GPT-2, no single block passed
the mitigation criterion on the matched trigger-free repair data.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, model repair, early exit, GPT-2
\end{IEEEkeywords}
